mcqs.question: Why does delta sync (sending only changed blocks) produce such a large bandwidth reduction over full-file re-upload for typical edit patterns?
options: Because most edits touch only a small fraction of a file's bytes, so re-sending the whole file wastes bandwidth proportional to file size rather than to the size of the edit
Because delta sync compresses files more efficiently than any other method
Because full-file re-upload is technically impossible for files over 1MB
Because block-level sync eliminates the need for a metadata service entirely
mcqs.explanation: The saving comes from sending bytes proportional to the edit size instead of the whole file — a few KB changed out of a multi-megabyte file. It's not about compression efficiency, full-file upload is entirely possible for large files (just wasteful), and a metadata service is still needed to track which blocks make up each version.

mcqs.question: Why do most real file-sync systems use content-defined chunking instead of fixed-size chunking?
options: Content-defined chunking is easier to implement than fixed-size chunking
Fixed-size chunking cannot be used for files larger than a few megabytes
Content-defined chunking has block boundaries based on the data itself, so an insertion only invalidates the blocks actually touched instead of shifting every subsequent block
Content-defined chunking always produces smaller total storage than fixed-size chunking regardless of edit pattern
mcqs.explanation: Fixed-size chunking's fatal flaw is that a single inserted byte shifts every block boundary after it, breaking dedup for the rest of the file. Content-defined chunking picks boundaries from the data itself, so an edit only affects nearby blocks. It isn't simpler to implement, fixed-size chunking works at any file size, and storage size depends on edit pattern, not a blanket guarantee.

mcqs.question: Why do most consumer file-sync products default to keeping both versions as a 'conflicted copy' rather than picking one automatically by last-write-wins?
options: Last-write-wins is technically impossible to implement in a distributed system
Conflicted copies use less storage than last-write-wins
Users are legally required to review every conflict manually
Last-write-wins silently discards one user's edit, while keeping both versions never loses data even though it occasionally shows an extra file
mcqs.explanation: The conflicted-copy approach trades a minor UX annoyance (an extra file to reconcile) for a hard guarantee that no edit is silently lost — last-write-wins can quietly discard real work. Last-write-wins is entirely implementable, just risky; conflicted copies use more storage, not less; and there's no legal mandate here, it's a product design choice.

mcqs.question: What's the core flaw in re-uploading an entire file on every save, even for a small edit?
options: Bandwidth and latency cost scale with total file size on every save, not with the size of the actual edit, which gets steadily worse as files grow and get edited more often
Full re-upload cannot preserve file permissions correctly
It is only a problem for files stored in the cloud, never for local-only files
It requires a completely different API design than chunked sync
mcqs.explanation: The core flaw is the cost mismatch: a one-line change still pays the bandwidth and time cost of the entire file, which compounds badly for large, frequently-edited files. It's unrelated to permission preservation, it's specifically a cloud-sync bandwidth problem (not a local-file issue), and the API can stay similar in shape — chunking changes what travels, not the call pattern itself.
